extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of science; readers assessing Bacon's scientific work
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the scientific knowledge, methods, and errors of a historical figure (Francis Bacon) in the context of contemporaneous science. Focuses on awareness of prior work, experimental rigor, conceptual clarity, and treatment of new theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with contemporary scientific literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon was ill read in the history of these branches of learning (and yet it was in this direction that science was making the most real and rapid advances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator should check whether the author engages with or cites the important contemporaneous works and inventions (examples cited: Napier's Logarithms (1614), Gunter's Canon (1620), Robert Napier's and Briggs's tables (1618), editions/translations such as Edward Wright's 1616 translation). Lack of mention of major works is a negative indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of ideas and ability to apprehend problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Where he could not readily follow the steps of the investigation, he could hardly appreciate the value of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the thinker clearly apprehends the nature of problems to be solved and can follow or reconstruct investigative steps; unclear ideas that prevent appreciating results indicate a serious defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and incorporation of established prior contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing the progress of Mechanics, he makes no mention either of Archimedes himself, or of Stevinus, Galileo, Guldinus, or Ghetaldus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good scientific writing/assessment should acknowledge and engage with major prior contributors (e.g., Archimedes, Galileo). Omissions may signal lack of acquaintance or failure to situate work in its lineage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of key theoretical advances (specific disciplines)
rubrics_metrics.description: He makes no allusion to the theory of Equilibrium. He overlooks the theory of the acceleration of falling bodies (Galileo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator should verify knowledge of central theories in the field (mechanics, hydrostatics, astronomy); failure to reference foundational theories weakens scientific credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design rigor and control of confounding factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In making an experiment of his own to ascertain the cause of the motion of a windmill, he overlooks an obvious circumstance which makes the experiment inconclusive, and an equally obvious variation of the same experiment which would have shewn him that his theory was false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether experiments are designed to rule out confounders and include decisive variations; omission of obvious controls or variants that would falsify hypotheses is a methodological flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of factual/astronomical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: He speaks of the poles of the earth as fixed, in a manner which seems to imply that he was not acquainted with the precession of the equinoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check factual correctness on established astronomical/geophysical facts (precession, motion of poles). Mistakes in basic facts indicate gaps in competence for related arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scepticism toward superstition and unempirical doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: He is evidently a believer, not only in Natural but Judicial Astrology, though, it must be owned, with a certain amount of hesitation and discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author discriminates between superstition and empirically grounded claims; uncritical acceptance of astrological or magical beliefs counts against scientific judgement, though historical context should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualizing speculative beliefs within contemporaneous norms
rubrics_metrics.description: An error... which was shared with Boyle... may well be pardoned to Bacon. An error... which was shared with contemporaries may be treated with less severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging historical figures, consider whether speculative beliefs were common among qualified contemporaries; contextualization can moderate the severity of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to credulous acceptance due to optimism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's very hopefulness, and his sanguine expectations of what nature had in store... may have rendered him peculiarly liable to be imposed on by these 'old wives' fables.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether optimism or exaggerated expectations led to credulous acceptance of unreliable reports or practices; intellectual caution is a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to engage with and adopt major paradigm changes
rubrics_metrics.description: But far the most important ... of Bacon's scientific errors was his persistent rejection of the Copernican theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate readiness to consider and, when warranted, adopt major theoretical reforms (e.g., heliocentrism). Persistent refusal without sufficient grounds is a significant professional failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and rhetorical balance in discussing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: His language is not that of 'positive disdain'; he proposes the alternative between the diurnal motion of the earth and that of the heavens as a subject of serious enquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author treats competing hypotheses with appropriate candour and discriminating tone (serious enquiry vs. dismissive rhetoric). Civility and openness to alternatives are positive markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of cogent arguments when rejecting a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Descriptio Globi Intellectualis Bacon actually advances some very cogent reasons against the Copernican theory, as it was then stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting established or emerging theories, good practice is to present cogent, reasoned objections rather than mere dismissal; evaluate quality of counterarguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that theoretical conception precedes experimental proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To be proved by experiment, a law must be conceived and imagined. To be put under discussion, it must be proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the thinker conceives testable laws/mechanisms before attempting experimental verification; ability to propose explanatory laws is prerequisite to experimental testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the mathematical/observational basis for theories
rubrics_metrics.description: By investing Copernicus with a system which requires Galileo, Kepler, and Newton to explain it... the modern astronomer refers the want of immediate acceptance of that system to ignorance, prejudice, and over adherence to antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether acceptance of a theory is supported by available mathematical/observational evidence and whether the proponent supplies necessary quantitative or observational backing; absence of such support explains reasonable reluctance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to revising opinion with changing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even Bacon was sufficiently moved by [Galileo's discovery of Jupiter's satellites] to include among his affirmations...; in De Augmentis, published in 1623, he pronounces himself far more positively [against Ptolemaic suppositions].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the scientist updates positions in light of new observations or stronger arguments; intellectual flexibility is a positive trait.
